promptText: Twitter and an internal team-status tool both reduce to the same functional requirement, 'users can post a short message,' yet their production architectures look nothing alike. What actually explains the divergence?
options: Their non-functional requirements differ by orders of magnitude (scale, latency target, consistency tolerance), and it is those requirements, not the shared functional requirement, that actually determine architecture
Twitter's messages are technically longer than the internal tool's, requiring a fundamentally different data model
The functional requirement can only be satisfied by a NoSQL database for Twitter, while the identical requirement can only be satisfied by a relational database for the internal tool
Internal tools are architecturally required to run on a single on-premises server, unlike public-facing products
explanation: Functional requirements describe what a system does, but non-functional requirements (scale, latency, availability, consistency) are what actually drive architecture; Twitter's need for hundreds of thousands of reads/second with eventual consistency versus the internal tool's small, strictly-consistent single-server load is entirely a non-functional distinction, not a functional one.

promptText: A CPU-bound service runs on a single instance. Why might doubling that instance's CPU and RAM (vertical scaling) actually be the more expensive long-term choice than adding more commodity instances (horizontal scaling), even though it requires no architectural change?
options: Vertical scaling follows a non-linear cost curve where doubling one machine's capacity costs far more than double, and it still leaves a hard ceiling and a single point of failure, whereas horizontal scaling's cost is roughly linear and removes that single point of failure
Vertical scaling always requires rewriting the application in a different programming language
Horizontal scaling eliminates the need for a load balancer once enough instances are added
Vertical scaling cannot be performed unless the service has already been made stateless
explanation: Vertical scaling's cost curve is non-linear and bounded by the largest machine money can buy, and it remains a single point of failure no matter how large the machine gets; horizontal scaling costs roughly linearly per added machine and removes the single-point-of-failure risk, which is why it is generally the better long-term lever despite its added architectural complexity.

promptText: A team "fixes" a bug where users lose state after being routed to a different instance by enabling sticky sessions at the load balancer, instead of externalizing session storage. What has this actually done?
options: It reintroduces the single-point-of-failure problem horizontal scaling was meant to remove — a pinned instance's crash or restart still loses that user's session, and even load distribution and clean instance replacement both become harder
It permanently fixes the bug, because the load balancer itself now stores the session data for every user
It makes the application tier stateless by definition, since the load balancer is handling routing consistency on the application's behalf
It has no effect on scalability or failure handling, only on raw per-request latency
explanation: Sticky sessions mask the symptom by pinning a user to one instance, but that instance is still the sole holder of the user's session, so its failure still loses that session, load can no longer be balanced evenly, and the instance can't be freely drained or replaced — the underlying stateful-routing bug is fully intact, not fixed.

promptText: A team provisions capacity for exactly the average QPS computed from DAU and actions-per-day, with no peak factor applied. What is the likely outcome, and what should capacity have been sized against instead?
options: The system will be routinely overwhelmed, because real traffic concentrates in predictable peaks well above the average; capacity should instead be sized against peak QPS, commonly average QPS multiplied by a 2x-3x peak factor
Nothing changes in practice, because average QPS and peak QPS are numerically identical for any well-behaved consumer product
The system will be fine regardless, as long as the database is horizontally sharded
Average QPS is actually a more conservative, higher figure than peak QPS, so provisioning against it is the safer choice
explanation: Traffic is never uniform across a day, so designing against the average is, by construction, under-provisioning for a large share of real traffic patterns; the peak factor exists precisely to convert an average into the number that should actually drive capacity planning.

promptText: A service keeps a small, plain in-memory HashMap on each instance caching a rarely-changing configuration value, re-fetchable from a shared source. Does this violate the statelessness principle?
options: No — because the data is cheaply re-derivable from a shared source of truth and correctness doesn't depend on every instance holding an identical copy at every moment, this is acceptable local-only state, unlike a user's session data
Yes — any local, in-memory data at all on an application instance violates statelessness by definition
No — statelessness only ever applies to data written to local disk, never to data held purely in memory
Yes, but only because a HashMap specifically is not thread-safe, not because of where the data is held
explanation: The test for whether local state violates statelessness is whether correctness depends on every instance seeing the same value; a disposable, re-derivable optimization like a cached configuration value is fine to keep local, whereas state like a user's session (where disagreement between instances causes a real user-visible bug) must be externalized.

promptText: Why is it important to treat a cache sitting in front of a database strictly as "an optimization, not the system of record"?
options: If the cache is lost entirely, the system should fall back to the database and remain correct, just slower — a design where losing the cache produces incorrect results has mistakenly made the cache part of the authoritative data store
Because caches are, by definition, incapable of ever holding data more recent than what is currently in the database
Because a cache that also served as the system of record would remove the need for a database entirely
Because treating a cache as a system of record would prevent a load balancer from distributing traffic evenly across instances
explanation: The database holds the authoritative data and the cache holds a copy purely for speed; if clearing or losing the cache ever produces wrong answers rather than just slower ones, the cache has silently become part of the source of truth, which is a design defect rather than a performance optimization.

promptText: A team doubles the number of stateless application instances behind the load balancer to address complaints that pages feel slow. Requests-per-second handled goes up, but individual page load times stay exactly the same. Why?
options: Horizontal scaling raises the throughput ceiling by adding concurrency, but it does nothing to shorten any single request's own critical path; per-request latency only falls by fixing the slow step inside that path, such as a slow query or downstream call
Per-request latency and throughput are mathematically the same metric, so improving one must always improve the other by an equal amount
This can only happen if the load balancer is misconfigured, since adding instances should always reduce latency proportionally
This can only happen if the newly added instances are secretly stateful
explanation: By Little's Law, throughput equals concurrency divided by latency — adding instances increases available concurrency and therefore throughput, but latency is set independently by each request's own critical path, so a slow downstream dependency keeps capping per-request latency no matter how many instances are added.

promptText: A service reports 50ms average latency, yet users still describe the product as feeling slow. What metric is most likely being missed, and why does it matter more here than the average?
options: Tail latency (p95/p99/p99.9) — an average can look healthy while a meaningful fraction of requests take seconds, and at real scale that tail represents a large absolute number of visibly bad user experiences
Total throughput — an average latency figure is only meaningful when reported alongside throughput in the exact same unit
Database disk usage — latency complaints are, in practice, always caused by the database running low on disk space
CPU utilization — latency is mathematically derivable directly from CPU percentage alone
explanation: Production systems are judged on tail latency because the slow outliers hidden behind a healthy average are disproportionately visible and damaging to perceived reliability, especially once scale turns even a small tail percentage into a large number of affected users.

promptText: Why does establishing a system's read/write ratio during scoping materially change its architecture, comparing a news feed to a metrics-ingestion pipeline?
options: A read-heavy system like a news feed benefits enormously from caching and read replicas that absorb load before it reaches the primary store, while a write-heavy system like metrics ingestion gets little benefit from read-side optimizations and instead needs the write path itself optimized, such as batching or write-partitioning
The read/write ratio only determines which programming language the backend should be written in
Systems with a high read/write ratio should disable caching entirely, since caching only helps write-heavy workloads
The read/write ratio determines whether the service must use TCP or UDP, independent of any other design factor
explanation: The read/write ratio directly determines where load actually concentrates; a read-dominated workload is best served by shielding the primary store with caches and replicas, while a write-dominated workload needs the write path itself scaled, since read-side techniques do little for it.

promptText: How should an engineer decide whether a given request flow actually needs a message queue, rather than adding one by default?
options: Identify whether there is genuinely asynchronous work that doesn't need to complete before the response is returned, such as sending a notification email; if every step in the flow is required to produce the response itself, a queue adds operational complexity with no decoupling benefit
A message queue should be added to any system handling more than one request per second, regardless of what work it performs
A message queue is required whenever a system runs more than one application instance, purely to coordinate between them
A message queue replaces the need for a database, since it durably stores all application state on its own
explanation: A queue earns its place only when there is real asynchronous work the user-facing path doesn't need to wait on; adding one without that justification is exactly the reflexive over-engineering this chapter warns against, since every added component is also added operational surface area to run and monitor.

promptText: A candidate proposes sharding the primary database before any scale estimation has been done. What is the strongest pushback, and what evidence would justify proceeding with sharding instead?
options: Sharding adds real ongoing complexity — shard-key routing, harder cross-shard queries, rebalancing — so it should wait until estimated or measured write throughput and storage actually approach what a single well-provisioned instance can sustain; the pushback is about missing justification, not sharding being wrong in general
Sharding should never be used in any system, since a single database instance can always be scaled vertically instead
Sharding is only valid once a system has already adopted a message queue, because the two are architecturally dependent on each other
The only requirement to justify sharding is having more than one engineer available to maintain the extra complexity
explanation: The objection to premature sharding isn't that sharding is inherently wrong — it's that its real operational cost is only worth paying once numbers show a single instance's throughput or storage ceiling is genuinely being approached, which is exactly the distinction between rejecting a valid future tool and rejecting its introduction without evidence.

promptText: Why does a horizontally-scaled service need to store user-uploaded files in object storage (e.g., S3) rather than the local disk of the instance that received the upload?
options: A file written to one instance's local disk is invisible to every other instance behind the load balancer, so a later request for that file routed to a different instance would fail to find it — the same statelessness requirement that governs session data applies equally to uploaded files
Local disks are physically incapable of storing binary file data larger than a few kilobytes
Object storage is required specifically because local disks cannot be encrypted at rest
Storing files locally would prevent the load balancer from performing health checks on that instance
explanation: Any data that must be visible beyond the single instance that first handled a request — sessions, uploaded files, anything a future request might depend on — has to live in a shared external store; a file stranded on one instance's local disk reproduces the exact stateful-routing bug statelessness is meant to prevent.

promptText: A payment balance and a social media "like" count are both, functionally, "display a number," yet an experienced engineer would likely pick very different consistency models for each. Why?
options: The cost of being wrong differs by orders of magnitude — a stale payment balance can cause real financial harm, justifying strong consistency even at some cost to availability or latency, while a stale like-count causes no meaningful harm, justifying trading strict consistency for higher availability and throughput
Payment balances must use a NoSQL database because financial data volumes are always larger than social engagement data
Like counts require strong consistency because users notice even a single-count discrepancy, unlike payment balances
The two features aren't actually comparable, since one is a write path and the other is a read path
explanation: This decision is made per-feature based on the actual cost of being wrong, not applied uniformly across a system: a payment balance should prefer correctness even if that occasionally means rejecting a request during a coordination delay, while a like-count should prefer availability and low latency since a slightly stale count is harmless and quickly self-corrects.

promptText: A system's production metrics diverge significantly from its original back-of-the-envelope estimate shortly after launch. What is the correct way to investigate this, rather than simply discarding the original estimate as a mistake?
options: Treat the estimate as a hypothesis: check whether the underlying assumptions (actual DAU, actions per user, read/write ratio, peak factor) matched reality, and whether the bottleneck is actually located where the estimate assumed it would be, replacing each wrong assumption with real telemetry
Immediately re-architect the entire system around a different database, since any mismatch between an estimate and reality means the whole design was wrong
Ignore the discrepancy as long as the system isn't currently down, since estimates are only useful before launch and have no further value afterward
Conclude that back-of-the-envelope estimation is not a useful technique and switch exclusively to load testing for all future capacity planning
explanation: A back-of-the-envelope estimate is a hypothesis built on assumptions (actions per user, peak factor, and so on) that real usage can validate or contradict; the productive response is to find exactly which assumption was wrong and update the model with measured data, not to abandon estimation as a discipline or overreact with a full rebuild.

promptText: A service shows plenty of spare CPU headroom on every instance, yet its throughput is still capped well below what that CPU capacity should allow. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Throughput is bound by Little's Law against a different resource than CPU — commonly a database connection pool, a downstream API's rate limit, or an internal lock serializing access to a shared resource — and that other resource's headroom, not CPU, is the real constraint
The service must be stateful, since only stateful services can become throughput-limited while CPU usage remains low
Spare CPU headroom always means the true bottleneck is network bandwidth between the client and the load balancer
This pattern only occurs when vertical scaling has mistakenly been applied to a fleet that was meant to scale horizontally
explanation: Little's Law applies to whichever resource is actually the binding constraint on concurrency, and CPU headroom says nothing about whether that other resource — a saturated connection pool is a common culprit — has headroom too; this is exactly the kind of mismatch that connection-pool and thread-pool metrics are meant to surface before concluding more CPU or more instances would help.
